title: Theraflu and Alcohol: Is It Safe? Nighttime vs Daytime Risks
excerpt: Can you drink on Theraflu? How its acetaminophen and diphenhydramine interact with alcohol, whether Theraflu contains alcohol, how long to wait, and when to get help.
metaDescription: Can you drink on Theraflu? How its acetaminophen and antihistamine interact with alcohol, whether Theraflu has alcohol, and how long to wait.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** it's best not to drink while you're taking Theraflu. Most Theraflu products contain a full dose of **acetaminophen** (the drug in Tylenol), and many also contain a sedating antihistamine like **diphenhydramine** (the drug in Benadryl). Alcohol makes both of those riskier. Acetaminophen and alcohol both load your liver, and diphenhydramine and alcohol both slow down your brain, so together they can leave you far drowsier and more impaired than either would alone. One drink with one packet is unlikely to cause a crisis in a healthy adult, but the safer plan is to skip alcohol while you're dosing and for most of a day after your last dose.

**The quick rules:** Don't use a Theraflu hot drink as a "hot toddy" by adding whiskey or rum. Don't take Theraflu Nighttime on a night you've been drinking. Don't stack Theraflu with Tylenol, NyQuil, DayQuil, or any other product that contains acetaminophen. If you have 3 or more drinks a day on a regular basis, ask a doctor or pharmacist before using any acetaminophen product. If you think you or someone else took too much, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US) right away, even if they feel fine.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and label guidance. It is not a substitute for a doctor or pharmacist who knows your health history. **Talk to your doctor or pharmacist before combining Theraflu with alcohol if** you drink 3 or more drinks most days, have liver disease, high blood pressure, heart disease, glaucoma, or trouble urinating from an enlarged prostate, take antidepressants (especially MAOIs) or other sedating medicines, or are pregnant or breastfeeding. **Get help right away** (call 911 or Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 in the US) if someone is very hard to wake, is breathing slowly, is confused, has a racing or pounding heart, or may have taken more than the labeled amount of acetaminophen. In an emergency, call 911.

## What's Actually in Theraflu?

Theraflu isn't one drug. It's a family of cold and flu products, most famously the powder packets you stir into hot water, plus caplets and liquids sold under names like ExpressMax. Formulas vary by product and change over time, so the Drug Facts box on your own box is the final word. But most Theraflu products are built from the same handful of ingredients:

| Ingredient | What it does | Found in | How it interacts with alcohol |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Acetaminophen** | Pain and fever reliever | Most Theraflu products, daytime and nighttime | Both are processed by the liver. The label carries a severe liver damage warning for people who have 3 or more drinks every day. |
| **Diphenhydramine** | Sedating antihistamine (also helps runny nose and cough) | Nighttime formulas | Both are sedatives. The label warns that alcohol may increase drowsiness. |
| **Dextromethorphan (DXM)** | Cough suppressant | Daytime "cold and cough" formulas | Can add to alcohol's dizziness, drowsiness, and poor coordination, especially at higher doses. |
| **Phenylephrine** | Oral decongestant | Most daytime and nighttime formulas | Little direct interaction, but it can raise blood pressure and heart rate, and there's little evidence it works when swallowed (more below). |
| **Pheniramine** | Older sedating antihistamine | Some "flu and sore throat" formulas | Behaves like diphenhydramine: more drowsiness with alcohol. |

A typical nighttime powder packet, for example, pairs a large single dose of acetaminophen (often 650 mg, more than a regular-strength Tylenol tablet) with diphenhydramine and phenylephrine. A typical daytime packet swaps the diphenhydramine for dextromethorphan. That's why the answer to "can I drink on Theraflu?" depends a lot on *which* Theraflu you took.

## Why Theraflu and Alcohol Don't Mix: The Two Main Problems

### Problem 1: Acetaminophen and your liver

This is the most serious risk, and it's the same one covered in our full guide to [Tylenol and alcohol](/never-hungover/tylenol-and-alcohol). Here's the short version in plain words.

Your liver breaks down most of each acetaminophen dose safely. A small slice, though, is handled by an enzyme (called CYP2E1) that turns it into a toxic by-product named NAPQI. Normally your liver neutralizes NAPQI right away using an antioxidant called glutathione, and nothing bad happens.

Alcohol can tip that balance in two ways. Regular heavy drinking increases the amount of the enzyme that makes NAPQI, so more of each dose goes down the toxic route. Heavy drinking and poor eating also drain glutathione, so there's less capacity to clean up. When NAPQI builds faster than glutathione can handle it, liver cells get damaged.

That's why every over-the-counter acetaminophen product in the US, Theraflu included, carries a liver warning. It says severe liver damage may occur if you take more than the maximum daily amount, take it with other drugs containing acetaminophen, or have **3 or more alcoholic drinks every day** while using the product.

Acetaminophen is the leading cause of acute liver failure in the United States, and a large share of those cases are accidental: people taking a little too much over several days, often from more than one product at once. Cold and flu season is exactly when that happens. You take Theraflu for the aches, Tylenol for the headache, and NyQuil to sleep, and you've tripled up without realizing it.

### Problem 2: Sedation stacking

The second problem is drowsiness, and it mainly applies to the nighttime versions.

Diphenhydramine is a first-generation antihistamine. It crosses into the brain easily, which is why it makes people sleepy and why it's the active ingredient in many over-the-counter sleep aids. Alcohol is also a central nervous system depressant. Put them together and the effects add up: heavier drowsiness, slower reaction time, worse coordination, and more confusion than you'd get from either one alone. The Theraflu label itself tells you to avoid alcoholic drinks and warns that alcohol, sedatives, and tranquilizers may increase drowsiness.

For most people that means a groggier night and a foggier morning. But it can be genuinely dangerous if you drive, if you're older (older adults are more sensitive to diphenhydramine's effects on memory and balance), or if you've had a lot to drink. If you'd like to understand the antihistamine side in more detail, our piece on [Benadryl for a hangover](/never-hungover/benadryl-for-hangover) covers it.

## Theraflu Nighttime and Alcohol

This is the combination to take most seriously. A nighttime packet gives you acetaminophen *and* diphenhydramine at the same time, so both problems above apply at once.

The realistic risks for a social drinker who takes Theraflu Nighttime after a few drinks:

- **Much deeper sedation than expected.** You may be hard to wake, unsteady if you get up in the night, and foggy well into the next morning.
- **Next-day impairment.** Diphenhydramine's effects can linger, and alcohol's after-effects add to it. Don't drive the next morning if you still feel slow.
- **Worse sleep quality, not better.** Both alcohol and diphenhydramine can make you fall asleep faster but tend to disrupt the deeper, restful parts of sleep later in the night.
- **Liver load on a vulnerable night.** If you've been drinking heavily and haven't eaten, your liver is in a poorer position to handle a big dose of acetaminophen.

If you've been drinking and you need help with cold symptoms at bedtime, the safer route is to skip the nighttime packet that night, drink water, and use non-drug options such as a humidifier, saline spray, honey for cough (for adults and children over one), and extra pillows. Take the medicine the next night when you haven't been drinking.

## Theraflu Daytime and Alcohol

Daytime formulas don't contain diphenhydramine, so the sedation stacking is milder. They still usually contain:

- **Acetaminophen**, so the liver warning applies in full.
- **Dextromethorphan**, a cough suppressant that at normal doses is usually well tolerated but can cause dizziness and drowsiness. Alcohol can make those side effects stronger. At high doses, dextromethorphan causes dissociative effects, and combining that with alcohol is risky. Dextromethorphan should also never be taken with MAOI antidepressants, with or without alcohol.
- **Phenylephrine**, a decongestant that can nudge up blood pressure and heart rate. Alcohol can do the same in some people, and a night of drinking can leave you dehydrated with a racing heart. If that's familiar, see our guide to a [racing heart after drinking](/never-hungover/heart-racing-after-drinking).

So "daytime" doesn't mean "fine to drink on." It means one fewer sedative in the mix. The same "no more than one product with acetaminophen at a time" rule applies. For the closely related DayQuil formula, our [DayQuil and alcohol](/never-hungover/dayquil-and-alcohol) guide goes ingredient by ingredient.

## Does Theraflu Have Alcohol in It?

This is one of the most common questions, usually from people who know that NyQuil's original liquid contains alcohol.

**The popular Theraflu powder packets do not list alcohol (ethanol) as an ingredient.** You mix them with hot water, and the drink you end up with is alcohol-free. That's one reason people who avoid alcohol sometimes choose Theraflu packets over liquid nighttime syrups. Our guide to [alcohol-free cold medicine](/never-hungover/alcohol-free-cold-medicine) compares the main options.

A few caveats:

- **Check liquid and syrup versions.** Theraflu has sold several liquid formulas over the years, and inactive ingredients can change. Look in the "Inactive ingredients" section of the Drug Facts box for "alcohol" or "ethanol." If you need to avoid alcohol completely, for example for medical, religious, or recovery reasons, read the label of the exact product you buy, or ask a pharmacist.
- **"No alcohol in the bottle" isn't the same as "safe with alcohol."** Even an alcohol-free Theraflu packet still contains acetaminophen and, at night, a sedating antihistamine. The interaction problem comes from those active ingredients, not from alcohol in the product.

## The "Theraflu Hot Toddy" Myth

Because Theraflu is a hot drink, some people treat it like a hot toddy and add a shot of whiskey, rum, or brandy. Please don't.

The idea of a hot toddy for a cold comes from the comfort of a warm drink, honey, and lemon, plus the sleepy feeling alcohol brings. There's no good evidence that alcohol helps you fight off a cold or the flu, and it tends to dehydrate you and disrupt sleep, both of which work against recovery. We go through the evidence in [does alcohol help a cold?](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-help-a-cold).

Spiking Theraflu specifically is a bad version of that idea. You'd be combining acetaminophen and (in the nighttime version) diphenhydramine with alcohol in one mug, which is exactly the combination the label warns against. If you want a comforting hot drink, have the Theraflu on its own, or have hot water with honey and lemon and leave the medicine and the alcohol out of each other's way.

## How Long After Theraflu Can You Drink?

There's no official waiting period printed on the box, and anyone who gives you a precise number of hours that applies to everyone is guessing. What we can say:

- **Wait until the medicine has worn off.** Theraflu doses are typically spaced about every four hours, which tells you roughly how long each dose is designed to act. Diphenhydramine's sedating effects can last longer than that in some people, especially older adults.
- **A practical rule for most healthy adults** is to wait until the next day after your last dose, or at least 12 hours, before having a drink. Longer is better after a nighttime dose.
- **If you're still sick, don't drink at all.** You'll recover faster without alcohol, and you'll likely need another dose soon anyway.
- **If you drink 3 or more drinks most days,** the waiting time isn't really the issue. Talk to a doctor or pharmacist before using any acetaminophen product.

## Can You Take Theraflu After Drinking (or for a Hangover)?

It's the reverse question, and the answer is similar: it's not a good idea, and it's not a good hangover remedy.

- **Theraflu isn't designed for hangovers.** It targets cold and flu symptoms: congestion, cough, fever, aches. A hangover involves dehydration, poor sleep, stomach irritation, and the after-effects of alcohol breakdown. The acetaminophen might dull a headache, but that's about it.
- **Wait until the alcohol is gone.** Your body clears roughly one standard drink per hour, though this varies a lot. After a heavy night, there can still be alcohol in your blood the next morning.
- **Eat first.** Food helps your liver restock glutathione and is gentler on your stomach.
- **Skip the nighttime version entirely after drinking.** Adding a sedating antihistamine on top of leftover alcohol is the combination most likely to cause trouble.
- **Don't take it "pre-emptively" before bed** to head off a morning headache. You'd be adding acetaminophen while your liver is still busy with alcohol, often on an empty stomach, for a problem you might not even have.

If what you mostly have is a hangover, Theraflu is the wrong tool. Water, food, sleep, and time do more. Our [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) guide covers the habits with the best evidence.

## The Hidden-Acetaminophen Trap During Cold Season

This deserves its own section, because it's the most likely way a normal person ends up in trouble.

When you have a cold or flu, you might reach for several products at once. A lot of them contain acetaminophen:

- Theraflu (most versions)
- Tylenol and store-brand acetaminophen
- NyQuil and DayQuil liquids and capsules
- Many Mucinex, Robitussin, and Alka-Seltzer Plus "multi-symptom" products
- Tylenol PM and other "PM" pain-and-sleep products
- Some prescription painkillers, such as hydrocodone or oxycodone combinations

On every Drug Facts box, look for **acetaminophen**, **APAP**, or **paracetamol**. Use only one acetaminophen-containing product at a time, and add up every dose across a 24-hour period. The general upper limit for healthy adults is 4,000 mg in 24 hours, many labels direct lower, and Theraflu's own box tells you the maximum number of packets or caplets per day. Follow that number, and if you drink regularly, ask a doctor whether a lower ceiling makes sense for you.

Also watch out for doubling up on antihistamines. If you've taken Theraflu Nighttime, don't add Benadryl, NyQuil, Unisom, ZzzQuil, or a "PM" product on top. Many of these contain diphenhydramine or a similar sedating antihistamine. Our [NyQuil and alcohol](/never-hungover/nyquil-and-alcohol) guide explains how those formulas compare.

## A Note on Phenylephrine

Most Theraflu formulas include phenylephrine as the decongestant. In 2023, an FDA advisory committee concluded that oral phenylephrine at the standard over-the-counter dose doesn't work as a nasal decongestant, and in late 2024 the FDA proposed removing it from the list of approved oral over-the-counter decongestant ingredients. That process may change what's in cold medicines on the shelf, so check your box.

For drinkers, the practical point is modest. Phenylephrine doesn't have a major direct interaction with alcohol, but it can raise blood pressure in some people, and it doesn't seem to do much for congestion when swallowed. If stuffiness is your main symptom, a saline rinse or a medicated nasal spray may help more. If you have high blood pressure, ask a pharmacist which decongestant, if any, is right for you. Our [Sudafed and alcohol](/never-hungover/sudafed-and-alcohol) guide covers pseudoephedrine, the decongestant kept behind the pharmacy counter.

## Who Should Be Most Careful

You're at higher risk from the Theraflu-and-alcohol combination if you:

- Drink **3 or more drinks most days**, or binge regularly
- Have **liver disease**, hepatitis, fatty liver, or elevated liver enzymes
- Are **not eating much**, which is common when you're sick
- Are an **older adult**, since diphenhydramine is more likely to cause confusion, falls, and urinary problems with age
- Have **high blood pressure, heart disease, thyroid disease, diabetes, glaucoma, or an enlarged prostate** (these are on the Theraflu label's "ask a doctor" list for a reason)
- Take **other sedating medicines**, such as sleep aids, anxiety medicines, opioids, or muscle relaxants
- Take **antidepressants**, especially MAOIs, which must not be combined with dextromethorphan or phenylephrine
- Are **pregnant or breastfeeding**

If any of these apply, spend five minutes with a pharmacist. They can look at your full medication list and suggest a cold remedy that fits. Our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) also covers how common medicines interact with alcohol and supplements.

## When to Get Help Right Away

Most people who have a drink while taking Theraflu will just feel unusually sleepy. But call 911 or go to the emergency room if someone:

- Is very hard to wake, or can't be woken
- Is breathing slowly or irregularly
- Is confused, has a seizure, or is seeing things that aren't there
- Has chest pain, a pounding or very fast heartbeat, or a severe headache

**Call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222 in the US) if** you or someone else may have taken more acetaminophen than the label allows, even if they feel fine. Acetaminophen poisoning is sneaky. People can feel almost normal for the first day while damage is building, and the early signs (nausea, vomiting, sweating, feeling unwell) look a lot like a hangover or the flu itself. Later signs include pain under the right ribs, yellow skin or eyes, and dark urine. Hospitals have an effective antidote (intravenous N-acetylcysteine), and it works best when started early, so don't wait for symptoms.

## A Better Path: Let Your Body Recover

If you're sick, the most useful thing you can do is give your body a break: skip the alcohol, sleep, drink fluids, and use one cold remedy at a time as directed. You'll likely feel better sooner, and you avoid the liver and sedation risks entirely. If a social event lands in the middle of a cold, it's fine to go and drink something non-alcoholic.

When you're well again and back to drinking socially, some people use supplements to support their bodies around a night out. Here's an honest view:

- **DHM (dihydromyricetin)** is a plant compound studied for its effects on alcohol metabolism and the liver. Most of the research is from animal and lab studies, with limited human data. It's promising, not proven, and there is no good evidence that it makes it safe to combine Theraflu, acetaminophen, or diphenhydramine with alcohol. Don't use it as a reason to drink while you're on cold medicine. If you want to try it on nights when you aren't taking medication, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains timing and amounts, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands.
- For a broader look at liver-focused supplements and the evidence behind each, see our [best liver supplements guide](/never-hungover/best-liver-supplements).

As with any supplement, check with a doctor or pharmacist first if you take regular medication.

## The Bottom Line

- Most Theraflu products contain acetaminophen, and nighttime versions add the sedating antihistamine diphenhydramine. Both interact with alcohol.
- The nighttime formula plus alcohol is the riskiest combination because it stacks liver load and sedation at once.
- Theraflu powder packets don't list alcohol as an ingredient, but that doesn't make them safe to drink on.
- Never spike a Theraflu drink with liquor, and don't take it before bed after drinking "just in case."
- Use only one acetaminophen product at a time, and follow the daily maximum on the box.
- If you have 3 or more drinks most days, ask a doctor before using Theraflu or any acetaminophen product.
- If there's any chance of an acetaminophen overdose, call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 right away.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Can you drink alcohol while taking Theraflu?**

It's best not to. Most Theraflu products contain acetaminophen, which adds to alcohol's load on the liver, and nighttime versions contain diphenhydramine, which adds to alcohol's sedation. One drink with one dose is unlikely to cause serious harm in a healthy adult, but the label tells you to avoid alcoholic drinks, and the risk climbs quickly with more alcohol, more doses, or extra acetaminophen from other products. If you drink 3 or more drinks most days, ask a doctor before using it.

**Does Theraflu have alcohol in it?**

The popular Theraflu powder packets that you mix with hot water do not list alcohol (ethanol) as an ingredient. Liquid and syrup formulas have varied over the years, so check the inactive ingredients in the Drug Facts box of the exact product you buy, or ask a pharmacist if you need to avoid alcohol completely. Remember that an alcohol-free formula is still not safe to combine with drinking, because of the acetaminophen and antihistamine it contains.

**How long after taking Theraflu can I drink alcohol?**

There's no official waiting period. Theraflu doses are typically spaced about every four hours, but the sedating antihistamine in nighttime versions can linger longer. A sensible rule for most healthy adults is to wait until the next day, or at least 12 hours after your last dose, before drinking, and longer after a nighttime dose. If you're still sick enough to need the medicine, it's better to skip alcohol until you've recovered.

**Can I take Theraflu after drinking or for a hangover?**

It's not a good idea. Wait until the alcohol has cleared from your system (roughly one standard drink per hour, though it varies), eat first, and avoid the nighttime formula completely after drinking, since diphenhydramine and leftover alcohol add up. Theraflu isn't designed for hangovers anyway. Its acetaminophen may dull a headache, but it does nothing for dehydration, nausea, or poor sleep.

**Is Theraflu Nighttime worse with alcohol than Theraflu Daytime?**

Generally, yes. Nighttime formulas combine acetaminophen with diphenhydramine, a sedating antihistamine, so you get both the liver concern and strong sedation stacking with alcohol. Daytime formulas usually swap the diphenhydramine for dextromethorphan, which can still add to alcohol's dizziness and drowsiness but is less sedating at normal doses. Both still contain acetaminophen, so neither is safe to drink on.

**Can you put alcohol in Theraflu like a hot toddy?**

No. Adding whiskey or rum to a Theraflu drink combines acetaminophen and, in nighttime versions, a sedating antihistamine with alcohol in one mug, which is exactly what the label warns against. There's no good evidence that alcohol helps you recover from a cold or flu, and it can dehydrate you and disrupt sleep. Have the Theraflu on its own, or have hot water with honey and lemon instead.

**Can I take Theraflu and Tylenol together?**

Usually not. Most Theraflu products already contain a full dose of acetaminophen, the same drug that's in Tylenol. Taking both at once is one of the most common ways people accidentally exceed the daily acetaminophen limit. Use only one acetaminophen-containing product at a time, count every dose over 24 hours, and ask a pharmacist if you're unsure.

**What should I do if I mixed Theraflu and alcohol?**

If you had a drink or two with a single normal dose and feel only drowsy, stay home, don't drive, drink water, and sleep it off with someone nearby if possible. Don't take another dose until the alcohol has cleared. Call 911 if someone is very hard to wake, breathing slowly, confused, or has chest pain or a pounding heartbeat. Call Poison Control at 1-800-222-1222 (US) if more than the labeled amount of acetaminophen may have been taken, even if the person feels fine.
